heading: Coding in Cree, Michif and Inuktut
intro: Métis, nêhiyaw (Cree) and Inuit coders, scholars and organizations build programs and interfaces so their languages work on computers and phones. A keyboard layout, a font, a converter and even a programming language are all ways to communicate with a computer system, which is the outcome of this lab. Each connection names the people whose work it is, with a source for each claim.

connections.title: Delaney Lothian: apps for Cree Michif and Cree
connections.text: Delaney Lothian, a Métis woman from Lac Ste. Anne, studied computing science at the University of Alberta. She practises Cree Michif with older relatives. After taking an introductory Cree course, she found few Cree resources online and thought, "I know basic programming." She built a verb conjugation app for a dialect of Michif. Its source code is public, so communities can upload their own spreadsheet of verb conjugations. In her game Sound Hunters, Cree sounds play and players shoot the creature showing the matching letter or word. She says technology is "not supposed to replace the human element" and must be built with communities "rather than for them."

sources.title: Source of all claims about Delaney Lothian (Métis woman from Lac Ste. Anne; Michif verb conjugation app with public code and community spreadsheets; Sound Hunters; quotes): University of Alberta, Folio, Graduate student uses technology to support Indigenous language learning (Anna Holtby, March 10, 2021)

connections.title: Typing and searching in Cree syllabics
connections.text: The lab says a keyboard can type Cree syllabics once the right layout is turned on. One is the ᓀᐦᐃᔭᐍᐏᐣ (nêhiyawêwin, Plains Cree) syllabics keyboard for Android and iPhone. Its help page says "you type the way you say it in Cree." You press the sound that starts a syllable, and the keys change to show syllables beginning with that sound. Researchers tested it at the University of Alberta in Edmonton with three First Nations or Métis typists. The itwêwina online Plains Cree dictionary, made with the Maskwacîs Education Schools Commission, accepts searches in Roman letters or syllabics and plays words recorded by first language speakers in Maskwacîs, Alberta.

sources.title: Source of how the keyboard works ("you type the way you say it in Cree"; keys change after the first sound; for Android and iPhone): Keyman, ᓀᐦᐃᔭᐍᐏᐣ (Cree Syllabics) Keyboard Help (National Research Council Canada)

Source of the user test (University of Alberta, Edmonton; three First Nations or Métis participants): Eddie Antonio Santos and Atticus G. Harrigan, Design and Evaluation of a Smartphone Keyboard for Plains Cree Syllabics (LREC 2020 workshop paper)

Source of the dictionary claims (search in SRO or syllabics; Maskwacîs Education Schools Commission partner; pronunciations recorded by first language speakers in Maskwacîs, Alberta): Alberta Language Technology Lab, itwêwina Plains Cree Dictionary

National Research Council Canada: Intelligent Plains Cree dictionary and word formation project (ALTLab, Maskwacîs Education Schools Commission and Cree Literacy Network; Plains Cree syllabics converter)

connections.title: Inuktut on every screen
connections.text: The Government of Nunavut says syllabics now work on "all of the most popular computer software." To type in a Unicode syllabic font such as Pigiarniq, "you will need the font itself and a keyboard driver." On phones, people can download the Naqittautit keyboards. Unicode, it explains, makes writing syllabics "as reliable and trouble-free as typing in English." Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami (ITK) adopted Inuktut Qaliujaaqpait, a unified writing system based on the roman alphabet, in 2019. ITK's online converter takes text typed or pasted in one regional writing system and outputs it in another. It "does not translate words or meanings": it only converts the letters.

sources.title: Source of the syllabics, Unicode, Pigiarniq font, keyboard driver and Naqittautit keyboard claims: Government of Nunavut, Computer Tools
Source of the 2019 adoption and "based on the roman alphabet": Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami, A Guide to Inuktut Qaliujaaqpait

Source of how the converter works (type, paste or upload text; regional systems including syllabics and Inuinnaqtun; "does not translate words or meanings"): Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami, Inuktut Qaliujaaqpait Converter
Nunatsiaq News: ITK launches Inuktut text conversion tool (Meral Jamal, November 3, 2022; Natan Obed and Conor Cook of ITK quoted)

connections.title: Cree#: code told as a story
connections.text: Jon Corbett, a nehiyaw-Métis computational media artist, computer programmer and professor at Simon Fraser University, created acimow/Cree#, a coding language that uses nehiyaw syllabics. He says languages like JavaScript, Python and HTML "prioritize the interests of Western cultures." In Cree#, programming operations are tied to cultural metaphor, and "you need to reformulate the code as story." A loop that adds a blanket each time it repeats can be told as "for five winters add one blanket to the inside of the canoe," where the canoe is a container holding blankets. Corbett says "Being able to program using an ancestral language is vital to the survival of such languages."

sources.title: Source of all claims about Jon Corbett and acimow/Cree# (nehiyaw-Métis; uses nehiyaw syllabics; code as story; blanket and canoe loop; quotes): Simon Fraser University, Scholarly Impact of the Week, Cree coding decolonizes computer programming (August 16, 2023)

try: Lesson 8 (Interfaces) says the same keyboard can type Cree syllabics once the right layout is turned on. Nunavut says typing in Pigiarniq needs the font and "a keyboard driver." Is the driver hardware or software? Which kind of interface is it, and which kind is the Cree phone keyboard? Then use Investigation 7 (Hardware and software setups): what would you add to a classroom laptop so a student can write in Cree or Inuktut?

Model ITK's converter with the IPO cycle from Lesson 6 and Investigation 6: what is the input, what is the process and what is the output? Now treat it as a function from Lesson 3: give it a descriptive name, list its inputs and describe its algorithm. Why does ITK say it "does not translate words or meanings"? What can the algorithm do, and what can it not do?

Corbett tells a loop as a story: "for five winters add one blanket to the inside of the canoe." Use Lesson 5 and Investigation 3 (Compare sequences): write the same job once as a plain sequence and once as a loop. Which is easier to change? Then use Investigation 5 (Decompose a task) to break Delaney Lothian's game Sound Hunters into smaller parts that could each be a function.

slide.title: Coding in Cree, Michif and Inuktut
points: Edmonton: Métis coder Delaney Lothian built a Michif verb app and a Cree sound game at the University of Alberta.
Alberta: a Plains Cree syllabics keyboard and the itwêwina dictionary, made with Maskwacîs partners, put Cree on screens.
Canada: Inuit use syllabics fonts and keyboard drivers; nehiyaw-Métis professor Jon Corbett codes in Cree#.
slide.notes: Use with Lesson 8 (Interfaces): the Cree syllabics keyboard and Nunavut's keyboard driver are real examples of the lab's keyboard layout sentence, one user to computer and one software to hardware. Pair ITK's converter with Lesson 6 (The IPO cycle) and Investigation 6. Pair Corbett's blanket and canoe loop with Lesson 5 (Sequences, loops and conditionals) and Investigation 3. Delaney Lothian's apps suit Lesson 2 (Decomposition) and Investigation 5. Point students to the Ways of knowing section in the lab for sources and discussion prompts.

review_flags: Existing content: the only Indigenous content is one sentence in Lesson 8: "The same keyboard can type Canadian French accents, or Cree syllabics, once the right keyboard layout is turned on." It is repeated as a review note in the lab's Teacher notes (CS1.K9) and in the deck's interfaces slide notes. It is unsourced, but it makes a general technical claim, not a claim about a people. The Alberta connection now sources it (Keyman help page for the Plains Cree syllabics keyboard; Government of Nunavut for syllabics keyboards generally). Suggested optional rewording with a link: "The same keyboard can type Canadian French accents, or nêhiyawêwin (Plains Cree) syllabics, once the right keyboard layout is turned on." Approve, or keep it as is. The footer "Edmonton, Treaty 6 territory" is a land acknowledgement line and needs no source.

Corbett loop: the SFU page quotes "for five winters add one blanket to the inside of the canoe," but the code it shows, for (x=1;x<5;x++), runs four times, not five. I quoted only the spoken story and did not show or count the code. Please check you are comfortable with that. I also left out the SFU page's description of "digital smudging" (a start up routine named for a ceremony) because the brief says not to describe ceremonies; it could be mentioned only with Corbett's own framing if you want it. I could not load the Cultural Survival Quarterly article by Corbett himself ("Cree Coding in Cree"); the permission request timed out, so it is not cited. It would be a stronger first person source if you can open it.

Spelling: SFU writes "nehiyaw-Métis" and "nehiyawewin" without circumflexes; I kept their spelling for Corbett and used nêhiyawêwin elsewhere as the Keyman and itwêwina pages do. Please confirm. I did not translate acimow because the source does not.

Alberta keyboard: the keyboard's help page credits National Research Council Canada and says the site was created by SIL Global; the 2020 paper is by Eddie Antonio Santos (NRC and ALTLab) and Atticus G. Harrigan (ALTLab). Neither page says whether the authors are Indigenous. The paper honestly concludes that "introducing a brand new paradigm for typing Plains Cree syllabics may not be ideal for the community." I left that out of the text to stay within length, but it would make a good Investigation 4 (Improve the code) discussion about testing with users. Want it added? I did not name the four Maskwacîs Nations or say Treaty 6 for Maskwacîs because no page I fetched states it.

Also found, not used: Justin R. Houle's 2018 University of Alberta MA thesis, a Star Chart Keyboard for Western Plains Cree syllabics on iOS (no identity stated on the page); Kaia MacLeod (James Smith Cree Nation) 3D printing a Cree Star Chart syllabics kit at the U of A Library, Edmonton, in 2020 (strong Edmonton and Cree authored, but it is about 3D printing rather than programs). INDIGital, an Indigenous Friends Association coding program for Indigenous youth at PÎYÊSÎW WÂSKÂHIKAN (Thunderbird House), Stanley A. Milner Library, in 2022, with Métis program manager Danielle Paradis and Elder in Residence Jo-Ann Saddleback (Taproot Edmonton and CBC). CBC says participants programmed robots to move in a fixed pattern and had an introduction to beading, but no source I fetched connects beading to algorithms, so I did not make that link. Any of these could replace or join the Edmonton connection.

Edmonton connection: Delaney Lothian is from Lac Ste. Anne; the Edmonton link is that she studied at the University of Alberta. The Folio article is from 2021, so her current role is unknown. Please confirm she is comfortable being named in a classroom resource, or swap in INDIGital.

Knowledge Keeper or guest: would you like to invite a Cree language teacher (for example through the Maskwacîs Education Schools Commission or the U of A Faculty of Native Studies), the Métis Nation of Alberta for Michif, or an Edmonton Inuit organization for Inuktut, to talk about language on screens? I have not contacted anyone.

Across the three computer science labs: the itwêwina Plains Cree dictionary (University of Alberta ALTLab with Maskwacîs speakers) also appears in the Design Process Studio Lab (user-centred design) and the Learning Machines Lab (speech synthesis), each time for a different idea. If that feels repetitive for a class doing all three, tell me which lab should keep it and I will find a different connection for the others.
